title: How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk
author: Adele Faber and Elaine Mazlish
theme: Children cooperate more willingly and grow more confident when parents acknowledge their feelings and replace blame, threats and lectures with respectful, descriptive language.
summary: Adele Faber and Elaine Mazlish were two mothers who attended parenting workshops inspired by the child psychologist Haim Ginott, then went on to run their own groups for parents. Their book collects what they learned into a friendly, workbook-style guide, full of cartoons, exercises and stories from real families.

The starting point is feelings. When a child is upset, the usual adult replies of denying, advising or reasoning tend to make things worse. Instead, the authors suggest listening with full attention, acknowledging with a simple word or sound, naming the feeling, and sometimes granting in fantasy what cannot be given in reality. A child who feels understood calms down faster and is more open to solving the problem.

Next comes cooperation. Rather than nagging or threatening, a parent can describe the problem, give information, say it in a single word, share their own feelings, or even leave a written note. These approaches invite children to take responsibility without feeling attacked.

The book questions punishment, arguing that it often breeds resentment rather than reflection. Alternatives include stating your expectations clearly, expressing strong disapproval without insulting the child, offering choices, showing how to make amends, and working through problems together by listing ideas and agreeing on one.

Later chapters cover encouraging independence by letting children make choices and respecting their struggles, and giving praise that describes what the child actually did rather than vague words like good or great. The final idea is to free children from labels such as lazy or shy, because children tend to live up, or down, to the roles we give them.
The tone is warm and forgiving. Parents will slip back into old habits, and the authors treat that as normal, offering practical skills that can be practised a little at a time.
takeaway: This week, when your child is upset, resist the urge to fix or correct, and simply name the feeling you see before saying anything else.

questions.q: What is the book's central message for parents?
options: Strict punishment is the surest path to good behaviour
Respectful communication that acknowledges feelings wins cooperation
Children should be left to solve every problem alone
Parents should avoid talking about feelings at home
questions.why: The authors show that acknowledging feelings and speaking respectfully makes children more willing to listen and cooperate.

questions.q: Whose work inspired the parenting workshops the authors attended?
options: Benjamin Spock
Maria Montessori
Jean Piaget
Haim Ginott
questions.why: Faber and Mazlish learned their approach in groups led by the child psychologist Haim Ginott.

questions.q: When a child is upset, which response does the book recommend?
options: Name the feeling the child seems to have
Tell the child there is nothing to be upset about
Give immediate advice on what to do
Explain why the child is being unreasonable
questions.why: Naming the feeling helps a child feel understood, while denying or advising usually escalates the upset.

questions.q: What does 'granting a wish in fantasy' mean?
options: Promising a reward later
Buying the child what they want
Expressing that you wish you could give them what they want, even though you cannot
Telling the child a bedtime story
questions.why: Imagining aloud what the child longs for shows understanding without giving in.

questions.q: Which is one of the book's skills for engaging cooperation?
options: Repeating the order louder
Describing the problem instead of blaming
Comparing the child to a sibling
Threatening to take away a toy
questions.why: Describing what you see lets the child figure out what to do without feeling attacked.

questions.q: Why do the authors question punishment?
options: It often leads to resentment rather than reflection on the behaviour
It takes too long to plan
Children enjoy being punished
It is always illegal
questions.why: They argue punishment distracts children with anger and revenge instead of helping them make things right.

questions.q: What kind of praise does the book recommend?
options: Frequent general words like 'great' and 'wonderful'
Praise only for winning
No praise at all
Describing specifically what the child did
questions.why: Descriptive praise lets children see their own effort and draw their own positive conclusions.

questions.q: How does the book suggest encouraging a child's independence?
options: Doing tasks for them so they succeed
Answering every question immediately
Offering choices and respecting their struggle
Avoiding all difficult tasks
questions.why: Letting children choose and acknowledging that a task is hard builds their confidence and self-reliance.

questions.q: What is the danger of labels like 'lazy' or 'shy'?
options: Children tend to live up or down to the roles they are given
They are too difficult for children to understand
They make children more ambitious
They have no effect at all
questions.why: The authors show that children often act out the roles adults assign them, so freeing them from labels opens new possibilities.

questions.q: In the book's problem-solving method, what do parent and child do after hearing each other's feelings?
options: The parent announces the decision
They postpone the issue indefinitely
The child is sent to their room to think
They write down ideas together and agree on one to try
questions.why: Joint brainstorming without judging ideas, then choosing one, gives the child a real stake in the solution.
